7.4.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
Meanwhile, the god said to the goddess, the daughter of the king of mountains:
“Let us go, O lovely lady, to bestow a boon upon the yakṣa, my devotee.
He is my devotee, O fair-hipped lady, whose sins have been consumed by austerity.
He is worthy, O mistress of the universe, to receive a boon from us.”
Having spoken thus, the lord of the world, together with the goddess,
went to where the yakṣa was sitting, emaciated and covered with veins.
And he granted him divine sight, by which he beheld Śaṃkara.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the yakṣa, O Vyāsa, slowly opening his eyes,
beheld the god accompanied by his retinue, seated on the bull-bannered [vehicle].
The god of gods said:
“I grant you a boon first: darśana throughout the three worlds,
and solidity of body; behold me, free from torment.”
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having obtained the boon and a body free from injury,
he bowed at his feet and stood with palms joined upon his head.

And he spoke then, urged by the lord saying, “I am the giver of boons”:
“O Lord, bestow upon me undistracted and undivided devotion toward you,
and the providing of food to the worlds, as well as imperishable leadership of the gaṇas,
so that I may always dwell in your abode, Avimukta.
O Lord of gods, I desire this supreme boon to be granted.”
The god of gods said:
“Freed from old age and death, completely devoid of all grief,
you will become the leader of the gaṇas, a granter of boons, worshipped by all,
unconquerable by all, endowed with the sovereign power of yoga,
and a provider of food to the worlds; you will become the guardian of the sacred field (Kṣetrapāla),
mighty, of great sattva, devoted to brahmins, and dear to me.

Also three-eyed, staff-in-hand (Daṇḍapāṇi), and a great yogin.
Udbhrama and Saṃbhrama shall be your two attendant gaṇas;
by your command, they will cause wandering and perplexity to the world.”
Sanatkumāra said:
Having thus made the yakṣa the lord of the gaṇas, O Vyāsa,
the divine Lord, the lord of gods, returned to his abode along with him.
Then, looking at the goddess, the god of gods whose emblem is the bull,
spoke in order to grant a boon to Mandara, who was performing austerity.
The god of gods said:
“O goddess with eyes like blossoming lotuses, O slender-waisted lady, I shall go
to Mandara, the foremost of mountains, wishing to confer the boon of grace.
Together with his wife, his sons, and his friends,
Mandara, the best of mountains, the foremost of ascetics, has taken refuge in me.

For five thousand divine years up to today, O Pārvatī,
the best of ascetics has practiced austerity toward me with his whole being.”
The goddess said:
“Take me too, O Lord of gods, to Mandara with its beautiful caves.
O god, without you, O Lord of the whole world, I shall find no delight.”
Then the god, the Supreme Lord, laughed and said to her:
“Avimukta must not be abandoned; how do you wish to go?”
The goddess said:
“I shall dwell right here and I shall also go to Mandara;
thus this abode, O god, will remain unabandoned (Avimukta).”
The god of gods said:
“It is just so, O fair-hipped lady, as you say, O Pārvatī.”

"Indeed, through divine power you go everywhere, O goddess, just as I do in all directions."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the blessed god Hara, mounting his bull that goes everywhere,
went to Mandara along with Umā, with Nandī, and with his retinue.
Having gone there, the Lord of the universe saw Mandara
performing supreme austerities, and having seen him, said:
"I am the giver of boons, O lord of mountains; I am exceedingly pleased with your tapas.
Choose whatever boon you desire; I grant all that to you."
Sanatkumāra said:
Addressed thus by Śarva, having seen the Lord of the three worlds
accompanied by Umā and Nandī, and having bowed to him whose mount is the bull,
having gazed again and again upon Hara, and again and again upon the Goddess,
he bowed again and again to the retinue and to Nandī.
Seeing him so overwhelmed, his eyes blurred with tears born of joy,
Hara once more gratified the mountain with a boon.
The God of gods said:
"Choose a boon; may it be well with you! O mountain, I am your granter of boons.
I wish to grant whatever you desire; choose a boon, O support of the earth!"
Mandara said:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased, O God of gods, O Lord of the universe,
I desire your dwelling upon me, together with Umā and along with your retinue.
I desire, O Lord of the gods of gods, by the touch of your feet always,

that myself be purified together with Umā and along with your retinue.
I desire no other boon from you here, O God, teacher of the universe!
Let this very boon be granted to me, O Lord of the universe!"
Sanatkumāra said:
"May it be so," the giver of boons then said to Mandara.
"With Nandī and together with the Goddess, I shall dwell always upon you.
And you, best of mountains, free from old age and death,
and impenetrable even to the thunderbolt, shall become so by my grace;
and charming to all living beings, adorned with gold and jewels,
thronged with hosts of apsarases, frequented by gods and siddhas."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then he created a great mansion there, made of Jāmbūnada gold,
surpassing thought in excellence, O Vyāsa; nowhere is there anything equal to it.
Even Brahmā has nothing like it, how much less anyone else!
Renowned by the name of Vṛṣa for its splendor, stature, and beauty.
Vyāsa said:
"O Blessed One, son of Brahmā, lord of all masters of yoga,
there is no satiety in me as the deeds of the God of gods are recounted by you.
How did that mighty bull, so beloved of great-souled Maheśa,
resounding loudly, attain the status of his mount?
Whose son was he? Whose grandson? And how was he born?
What was his tapas, and what its fruit? This I desire to know.
Formerly, a cloud was the mount beloved of Rudra;

The God of gods said:
'Become a cloud of the worlds; your success will be achieved.
Then you will nurture the worlds with nectar-like waters.'
Yajña said:
'If being a cloud brings auspicious welfare to the world,
may I bear you, the abode of lightning, upon my back.'

Severed into two pieces by the thunderbolt, that imperishable one invoked Śakra. / He said: "You possess great yoga; you are capable of uniting yourself."
By his yogic power Dadhīca rejoined his own body that had become so, / and went to Śarva for refuge. / Having propitiated the Lord of gods, he obtained supreme invulnerability, / bones as hard as a thunderbolt, impenetrability, and freedom from old age from Śaṅkara, / compassion for all beings, and great yogic power. / He returned to see Kṣupa, and friendship arose between the two again. / And the passion born of caste arose just as before: / that Kṣupa struck him with his left foot. / And taking the thunderbolt again, he struck him then. / But that thunderbolt caused him neither distress nor pain, O sage. / Then, realizing the invulnerability of that great-souled one, / Kṣupa approached Nārāyaṇa and propitiated him for a boon.

Yet, out of curiosity, I go to seek refuge with the guardians of the world. / Finding them powerless to act, I shall then go to Śaṃkara.”
Having spoken thus, the son of Cyavana ran toward Varuṇa; / and when he took refuge in him, the powerful lord granted him freedom from fear.
There, a terrible and frightful battle took place / between the god Viṣṇu and the wise Varuṇa for many years.
When Varuṇa was defeated, the son of Cyavana approached Yama. / He too granted him freedom from fear, [but] was defeated in battle by Viṣṇu.
Then he approached Agni, O Vyāsa; he too was utterly vanquished by him. / Then, taking a handful of kuśa grass, that son of Cyavana,
returned to his hermitage and cried out, “Stand! Stand! / For the sake of inquiry, I went for refuge to the guardians of the world.
They are all powerless; supreme strength resides in me alone! / Today your pride, arrogance, and whatever wondrous power you possess— / I will destroy all that! Stand now, O Janārdana!”

7.4.m: Dadhīca too, endowed with great fiery energy, performed austerity in his own hermitage, / terrible [tapas] consuming only air and water to win Mahādeva's favor. / Then, as he who had the brilliance of the sun was engaged in austerity, / the three-eyed Lord was pleased, and, being pleased, spoke thus: / The God of gods said: / 'O Cyāvana, O observer of vows, I am pleased by this austerity of yours. / Speak what you desire; it is already accomplished by me.' / Dadhīca said: / 'O Lord, if you are pleased and if a boon is to be given to me, / I wish for all the gods along with Viṣṇu to be conquered by you.' / Sanatkumāra said: / Then Hara, who dispels the distress of the bowed, the giver of boons, laughed / and said to Dadhīca, the best of seers: 'So be it.' / When that auspicious boon was granted by the three-eyed Lord, / the seer considered the enmity with Kṣupa to be ended.

Seeing him thus contemplating, the Lord whose banner bears the bull / said: 'Speak another boon, O vipra, and I will grant it to you.'
Dadhīca said: / 'Since this enmity has ended because of your granting of a boon, O Lord, / therefore let your place here be known by this name, O unborn one.'
The God of gods said: / 'This excellent place shall be renowned by the name Sthāneśvara, / extending for a krośa and filled with various flowers and creepers. / Whoever worships me here, having undertaken the supreme vow, / having fasted for three nights and properly bathed in the river, / and, endowed with righteousness, having fed a brahmin with oblation rice, / shall be freed from all sins and attain my world.

7.4.m:
[This] will come to pass, of that there is no doubt; hear also from me the fruit of this.
Whoever should stay here day and night, self-controlled and eating regulated food,
by him the unsurpassed vow of Sthāṇu will have been personally observed.
Freed from all sin, he will become an attendant-chief of mine,
named Akampana, mighty and endowed with the power of great yoga.
And whatever human being, practicing self-restraint or indeed disciplined,
should abandon his vital breaths [here], great is his fruit of merit:
freed from all sin and released from all fetters,
he becomes a lord of attendants equal to Nandin, capable of going everywhere.
Moreover, whoever, having stayed here at Sthāneśvara for one night, should consume [his sins] without remainder,
his mind completely freed from all sin, he shall become a most terrifying lord of attendants of mine.”
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, named “The Dispute between Kṣupa and Dadhīca,” in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.4.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
“At that very time, O Vyāsa, King Dakṣa Prajāpati,
the son of the Pracetases, performed a horse sacrifice.
There, impelled by mantras, the fire carrying the offerings
was then conveying the portions everywhere for the hosts of gods.
And the goddess, the daughter of the best of mountains, saw him conveying [them],
remembering that enmity and the cause of the curse.
And the mountain-born [goddess], prompting the ancient one, spoke to him
fittingly in sweet words, accompanied by reason:
‘You are the god of all the gods, their refuge and their shelter.
Without you, how does a sacrifice proceed, O protector of all gods?
This fire, O Bhava, is conveying the portions of the gods;
he is not [conveying] yours, O Maheśāna of great splendor! What is the reason?
An aim is not achieved through conciliation without prowess, O Lord!
This king, the son of the Pracetases, is foolish and arrogant;
remembering previous enmity, he will never give [your share] unless he is chastised.
Moreover, a boon was given by you to Dadhīca at that time, O Lord;
the time for that has come—let [action] be taken for that purpose!’”

7.4.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
“Addressed thus, O Vyāsa, the blessed Lord who bears the bull upon his banner
smiled and spoke to the goddess: ‘O lady of bright smiles, your father
in a previous birth, O fair-hipped, auspicious one, was the son of Prajāpati.
Testing my disposition, O goddess, do you speak [thus]?
For no passionate woman wishes sorrow upon her father in this world.’
Spoken to thus at that time, O Vyāsa, by the pure-souled god,
the goddess of wide eyes then knit her brows upon her forehead,
and in anger the brightly smiling one rubbed the tip of her nose with her hand.
As that nose was being rubbed, a woman of great radiance
was born, with a frown on her face, four fangs, and three eyes,
wearing armguards of leather and finger-protectors, clad in armor, wearing a girded belt,
having a sword, a bow, quivers, and a banner,
twelve-faced, ten-armed, slender-waisted, dark as gloom,
with firm breasts, broad hips, thighs like elephant trunks, imperishable.
The goddess with a lovely face addressed that goddess as Bhadrakālī.
Then she spoke to the god: ‘She has been created by me, O Lord;
you also create another suitable attendant. Homage be to you!’
Then the god looked upon his own radiant shoulder;
from it was born a divine man, as if burning up the three worlds,
his face adorned with knitted brows, equipped with leather armguards and finger-protectors,”

7.4.m: Armored, with quiver bound, holding arrows, sword, and bow, / three-eyed and four-armed, a youth of adamantine frame— / having been created, he bowed down, the troop-lord named Hari, / and with cupped hands addressed the God of gods together with Umā: / “Command, O Lord of gods, what I am to do, O pervasive Lord.” / Then the Blessed One spoke to Hari, the commander of the troops: / “Go, destroy this sacrifice of the son of Pracētas. / Together with Bhadrakālī, swiftly carry out this deed, O lord of the troops.” / Then the blessed god, wise, created lords of troops / of multifaceted shapes from his own limbs, able to assume any form at will. / He touched his arm properly, and from it were born mighty ones. / There were ninety hundred crores [of them] born of the Lord. / The Blessed One said to them: “O sinless ones, destroy the sacrifice!” / Sanatkumāra said:

7.4.m: Then the two, surrounded by that vast army, / went forth with roars like the ocean and rumblings like clouds and thunderbolts. / And the god, together with Pārvatī, staying near the hermitage of Raibhya, / watched that work of destroying the sacrifice by the troop-lords. / Sanatkumāra said: / The trees of Kanakhala stood near the gate of the Gaṅgā, / and there was a mountain with golden peaks resembling Mount Meru. / In that region, Dakṣa's sacrifice was taking place. / And the formidable army of the troop-lords arrived, led by Kālī. / Having arrived, all those exalted ones, radiant as blazing fire, / spoke to the patron of the sacrifice, the officiating priests, the sages, and the gods: / “We are indeed all followers of Śarva, the Supreme Self. / We have come here desiring shares; bestow the desired shares! / By austerity, by strength, or by restraint are [people] worthy of sacrificial shares, / or by majesty, or by yoga—by whatever means before you. / All of that is indeed in us as well; we too are share-takers. / If the gods are masters, and therefore have attained worthiness of shares— / in mastery, strength or austerity is the cause, no doubt of this; / both of those reside in us alone, and therefore our mastery is superior. / But if this is someone's command, O best of sages and gods: / ‘A share must be given to you [gods], but not to us,’ let it be stated! / Tell us who commands this, and then we will know.”

7.4.m: Thus addressed by Hari, all of them, led by the gods, / said: “The mantras are the authority regarding your share, O troop-lords.” / And the mantras said to the gods: “Your minds are overpowered by darkness, / since you did not offer sacrifice to Maheśvara, who is worthy of the first share.” / When, even though being addressed by the mantras, they still did not give shares, / the mantras then departed from there to the eternal realm of Brahmā. / Then the gods, Śakra and others, said to the troop-lords: / “[…] / having advanced, we will strike down in battle all of you who have come!” / Hearing their arrogant words, Hari, the vanquisher of foes, / laughing, spoke to all of them these forceful words: / “The mantras have not been accepted as authority by you who are arrogant with power; / because you acted violently, today I will destroy you who roar [in pride]. / Prompted together with the sacrifice, the officiating priests, and the shares, / and whatever power you possess, all of that will I destroy.” / Having spoken thus, the radiant, glorious Haribhadra / and the furious Bhadrakālī rushed against the gods. / And the enraged troop-lords, tearing up the sacrificial posts, hurled them away. / The troop-lords, all angered, seized the *hotṛ* priest along with the *prasthātṛ*, / and the horse, and hurled them into the current of the Gaṅgā; / and having bound the patron of the sacrifice with a snare, they led him away at their pleasure. / Others [seized] the altar, others the *kuśa* grass, others the ladles, and others the cups.

7.4.m:
They destroyed and threw down [the vessels], and set fire to the other sheds. / Then Haribhadra, blazing in spirit and undaunted, / paralysed Indra's arm as he raised it, and did likewise to the other gods. / His face furious, he struck Bhaga's eyes and Pūṣan's teeth / with the tip of his bow and knocked them out while [all] were watching. / And Viṣṇu's terrible discus, which had the radiance of the sun at the end of an age, / he paralysed with undaunted spirit; stationed in [Viṣṇu's] hand, it did not even stir. / And the Tuṣita gods, ready and longing for battle, / he struck down with a Vāyavya weapon and felled them to the earth. / And that flawless god bewildered all the other gods / arrayed for battle with his supreme weapon, the Mohana. / And whatever kings had arrived there desiring to see [the sacrifice], / he drove them all forcibly to their own homes by the power of his weapon. / Seeing the jars smashed, the sacrificial posts and arches broken, / and the great sheds set ablaze, the Sacrifice fled. / As it was running towards the sky in the form of a deer, / Hari fitted an arrow and decapitated it. / Then the valiant Vīrabhadra took another arrow / and pursued that Sacrifice as it fled in the form of a deer; / he reached it, bound and struck down, so that it attained equality with the constellations. / Sanatkumāra said: / Thus humiliated, O Vyāsa, by the gaṇas, by Kālī, / and by the god Hari, they all took refuge.

7.4.m:
Smiling, the Self of all, the creator of all, spoke words:
The God of gods said:
"I am not angry; you are forever very dear to me. / If I were angry, in the next moment there would be no life for you."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus, the god then, wishing the welfare of the gods, / caused all those gods to enter through yogamāyā,
into his own body, Mahādeva, in order to astonish them with his power. / Then they entered the body of the noble Īśvara.
They saw a wondrous universe endowed with seven worlds. / Having wandered through all those worlds, all filled with fear,
having gathered there, they saw the heroic Gaṇapa Pañcākṣa. / By him all those tigers among gods, unwearied, were cast upwards,
and having arrived in another world in an instant, / those fortunate ones saw a city resembling the sun,
surrounded by a vast rampart of crystal, / and with varied, wonderful crests shining brightly with jewels and gold.
Then, above that, those best of gods saw in its midst / an auspicious city of seventy million yojanas all around,
divine, surrounded by a silver rampart having the luster of the moon. / In the middle of it, further above, was a city extending for sixty million [yojanas],

Other trees there, O Vyāsa, are milky and full of great splendor; / all continuously flow with cow-like milk.
The entire ground is gem-studded with auspicious golden sands; / there are water springs and mountain cascades.
Among them there is no anger or greed, no fighting, hatred, or malice; / no delusion, no arrogance, nor are there other faults there.
In its middle was another auspicious city, extending twenty million [yojanas], / adorned with a rampart made of ruby.
Having passed by such cities, then the gods [saw a city] / extending ten million yojanas, encircled all around by fire,
having the appearance of the cosmic fire at the end of an aeon, terrible to look upon, a vast city; / without a gateway, divine, and boundless, those foremost gods beheld it.
Having seen it, they were seized with great wonder and fear. / To those lords of gods, whose faces were terrified and who were trembling, O Vyāsa,
the Gaṇapa Pañcākṣa said: "Let there be no fear in you, O gods!
This very vast, dreadful city surrounded by terrible fire / is to be seen by you, noble ones, for the sake of which you have come here."

7.4.m: [We take refuge in her] whose terrible fangs are white as the moon, a necklace, or water; who is victorious in battle; / who is hard to gaze upon, whose terrible glance is beyond thought; wide-eyed, wearing yellow silk garments; / whose staff bears a great trident, a bell, and a flag; who loves divine fragrance, ghee, and incense; / whose fierce hand holds the staff of death, a sword, and a shield; whose vessel is filled with omentum, blood, entrails, and fat; / who faces the southern quarter; who wears a charming golden fillet; whose eyes resemble the fire at the end of an aeon; who emits loud laughter; / who acts according to her own will; who is unpierced by the weapons of the bodiless god [Kāma]; who has a army of heroes; who is the famous river; / who dwells eternally on Mount Mandara; who abides in heaven; we take refuge in her, the longed-for one (?), / who tore apart the demon Mahiṣa; who tore apart Dundubhi; who slew Sunda; / who was death to Niśumbha; who creates a radiance shining like the moon, the sun, and fire; who bestows what is desired; / who removes grief, sorrow, and pain; sorrowless; fierce; dense; who brings an end to Death; / the vital strength of the sage, son of Jamadagni; and the queen of the king of kings; / charming, dreadful, the night, the science of governance; stability, desired perfection, the auspicious Kālarātrī; / Aparṇā, meditative absorption, the refuge; who loves dwelling on the king of mountains; who eternally abides in the Ocean of Milk; auspicious; / adorned with large tinkling bells; whose hair is dishevelled and stands upright; whose splendor has the hue of kindled fire and evening clouds; / wearing a finger-guard made of monitor-lizard skin; three-eyed; adorned with a garland interwoven with reddish lotuses in her matted locks; free from grief; / born from the spark of the eye of the foe of the bodiless god [Kāma]; adorned with a garland woven of golden wreaths; wearing a long, lovely braid; / endowed with renown and glory; having a multi-colored banner fastened with peacock plumes; passionate; the bringer of peace;

7.4.m: I ever take refuge in that one alone, who wears bracelets made of a hundred serpents; / who is drunk on the life-breath of great Daityas; whose limbs and hair are rough with the ashes of funeral pyres; whose great knees hang down and belly is swollen; / wearing a serpent as a sacrificial thread; whose ornaments are wet hands, half a face, raised eyes, and half a foot; / wearing a garland of various flowers hanging down from a great girdle-cord; / who delights in dancing to the fierce music of large drums that sound like great thunderclouds; / who loves songs, laughter, chatter, and joy; who transcends dwelling, living abroad, and residing through recitation, oblation, and fasting; / whose fierce essence accords with the essence known through great yoga; / firmness itself; whose bowstring and bell sound with fierce noise; / whose roar is sharp and terrible, resembling a great thundercloud, the fall of a thunderbolt, and the ocean; / the ritual act, and the initiation of the initiated; the wife of the uneven-eyed god; dwelling in half of Hara’s body; / I take refuge in the primordial, supreme Goddess, Pārvatī, born from the spark of his mouth; / the presiding deity of all branches of knowledge; the refuge; the embodiment of restraint, observance, and self-control; / the auspicious daughter of the ancestors, the daughter of the king of mountains; who brought an end to Dakṣa’s sacrifice; / who knocked out the teeth of the Sun when residing in half of Bhava's body; / who paralyzed the raised arm of Indra; who took away the hair of Viṣṇu; / whose great conveyance is harnessed to a great lion; Mahābhairavā; terrifying; the fire-stick [that brought forth] Skanda and the moon; / the foremost mother of the elephant-faced god; the fire-stick for the birth of Viśākha; / the producer of Nandin and Naigameṣa;

Sanatkumāra said:
Praised thus by the gods with joyful hearts,
and through Tryambaka's grace, the pleased Goddess spoke this to the gods: / 145
The Goddess said:
Go forth, all of you, freed from anguish; I am pleased with you, without a doubt.
Do not act in this way again, O gods, lest destruction befall you. / 146
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that god, the smiling, matted-haired, blue-and-red one,
the slayer of the gods' enemies, restored all the gods to their natural state. / 147
And the Lord of Gods said to them: "Go forth, freed from anguish;
and when a sacrifice is to be performed, then this [sacrifice] will indeed belong to you. / 148
Joined together with its head, O sons of Diti, by this mantra."
Then the God gave the Atharvan hymn and imperishable joining mantra,
and spoke this in a melodious voice: / 149
The God of Gods said:
Let this sacrifice attain parity with the constellations, O best of gods!
And let this god Hari, pursuing the deer, become its [protector]. / 150
Bhadrakālī, Hari, and these mighty attendants,
all of them will forever bring good fortune to you, O immortals! / 151
Sanatkumāra said:
Addressed thus by the Lord, those gods, together with Brahmā,
all bowed their heads and spoke these words to Śarva: / 152
"Let this best of sacrifices belong only to you, O Lord;
everything, O God, Lord of Gods, imperishable one, is worshipped... / 153

7.4.m:
Of the shares in all sacrifices, we give everything to you."
Addressed thus by all the gods, the Lord of Gods, the sovereign of deities, / 154
assumed a supreme, auspicious form consisting of all the gods.
Then, in the Great Lord, the gods saw their own selves: / 155
in his head, arms, thighs, and feet, in his bladder, hands, belly, and other limbs,
they saw the great-souled sages rich in austerity abiding. / 156
Having assumed that form, Śaṃkara then said to the gods:
"All of you great-souled ones are born from my body. / 157
Look at your bodies, which consist of me!"
Then, O Vyāsa, those deities saw the entire universe consisting of Rudra / 158
and also saw themselves, their minds struck with amazement.
Having thus revealed his power to them, the Lord of Gods / 159
said to the tigers among gods: "You have seen these manifestations.
Whichever form one worships endowed with supreme devotion, / 160
having taken that form, I receive his worship, O gods.
I have no need for sacrificial shares; the sacrificial shares are yours, O gods.
I grant them all [to you] today; go forth, all of you, freed from anguish!" / 161
The gods said:
"This supreme secret has been revealed by you to us, O God.
The mortal who understands this shall attain imperishable worlds. / 162
And this place, O Blessed One, known as Bhadreśvara,
shall be the best in the universe, the most holy of holy [places]. / 163
All around, for a yojana, is this eternal Rudrakṣetra.
One who dies here, O God, shall become a leader of your attendants, beloved to you. / 164

let that accrue here, O God, to a man who constantly worships. / 169
And whatever best of men shall abandon his life-breaths here,
he shall become a mighty attendant of Haribhadra." / 170
Sanatkumāra said:
Having said "So be it," the Blessed Lord Śarva, with Soma,
surrounded by hundreds of attendants, went to the lovely cave of Mandara. / 171
The gods, along with their king, also remained at that place in comfort,
while Brahmā and Viṣṇu went behind the God. / 172
Having gone a short distance with both of them, the Lord,
not very far away, then said: "Halt, O mighty Viṣṇu!" / 173
Then, bowing down to the feet of Hara, that best of men...

7.4.m: He stood leaning on a mango tree, and he became crooked (kubja). / Because Hari stood in that place leaning on a mango tree, / gazing at the Lord of gods, therefore that place became [known] / as Kubjāmraka, the prosperous sacred field of Viṣṇu, / holy, yielding the fruit of a thousand cows upon a nivartana [of land] of Viṣṇu. / Having gone not very far from there, the Lord again said to the Grandfather: / “Turn back,” O Vyāsa, and entered the sky. / When that god had ascended into the sky, Brahmā, with folded hands and upturned face, / having circumambulated [and] bowed, then departed. / Since there, while making circumambulation around Hara, / a turning (āvarta) of his own body was performed by that [god] of holy deeds, / therefore that lovely place became renowned as Brahmāvarta. / A man who bathes there attains the fruit of an aśvamedha sacrifice. / Having prepared the sacrificial caru here and fed the twice-born, / and then relinquishing his life-breaths, he would attain the world of Brahmā. / Then Brahmā, having approached along with the gods preceded by Viṣṇu, / performed the glorification of Paśupati at Bhadreśvara. / Having installed a liṅga there and performed a very splendid worship,

7.4.m: and having bathed in the Bhadrakarṇa pool, he went to heaven together with the gods. / Then Dakṣa spoke this to Brahmā as he was departing: / “O God, tell me who am asking, what ought to be done by me?” / The Grandfather said: / “Propitiate Śarva, the wielder of the great bow, the fierce one with matted hair. / Then you will attain the completion of the sacrifice and imperishable worlds.” / Sanatkumāra said: / Having been thus addressed in truth by the god Brahmā, O Vyāsa, / he set up a liṅga at Kanakhala and then worshipped Rudra. / When a divine hundred years of that Prajāpati were completed, / Mahādeva, smiling on the mountain summit, said to the Mountain's daughter: / “The son of Pracetas, O goddess, stands restrained in austerity. / Behold him, O ruler, established with mind focused on me!” / Then, having seen him subsisting on air, / worshipping Maheśvara in the liṅga with supreme devotion, / the delighted goddess, with joined palms, O Vyāsa, / said to the god, her husband, the Lord of all gods who is worshipped by all deities: / The goddess said: / “This fellow is low, wicked-minded, arrogant, proud, and evil-natured. / Fortunately, humbled by you, he has resorted to you alone for refuge. / Therefore, O Maheśvara, you ought to forgive this devotee of wicked disposition who has surrendered; / I propitiate you for his sake.” / The God of gods said:

7.4.m: “O goddess, you yourself grant him the desired boons as you please. / Permitted by me, O fair-browed one, bestow the boon upon him yourself.” / Sanatkumāra said: / Then those two rulers of the gods, united and surrounded by their own gaṇas, / said: “Behold us two, O Dakṣa, who are pleased, with divine vision! / O son of Pracetas, O highly fortunate one of great austerity, we two are givers of boons! / [...] / For the pacification of the curse, I grant you this desired boon: / That sacrifice of yours which was destroyed by the gaṇas—attain its fruit! / Assuming forms at will, glorious, become a gaṇeśa for me; / imperishable and immortal, free from sorrow and grief, / you will be, O highly fortunate one, close beside me.” / The goddess said: / “Listen again: what else should Maheśvara bestow? / Even if it is very difficult to grant, he will bestow the boon requested by you.” / Sanatkumāra said: / Having been thus addressed then by that daughter of the Himavat, / the wise Dakṣa, with folded hands, having bowed down, said this: / Dakṣa said: / “The god who is the maker of the origin and destruction of the three worlds, whom the foolish do not know, the single, unmanifest one, / the remover of inauspiciousness for devotees, holding the Pināka bow in hand—to that god we, together with our wife, have gone for refuge! / Who out of ignorance, due to demonic nature, and through excessive pride and delusion, was not indeed worshipped by us along with the Daughter of the Mountain—”

To that God, the Lord of gods, who in his anger gave me a curse, / we have gone for refuge, together with his consort. // 201
To that God who is the creator of the host of gods, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, / of the siddhas, the sons of Diti, the lords of dānavas, and humans, / of the spirits, domestic beasts, wild animals, birds, and snakes, / we have gone for refuge, together with his consort. // 202
To that God who in his wrath created the great lord of the gaṇas, / the lion-king, Hari of immeasurable power and form, / and his wife endowed with immeasurable virtues and majesty, / we have gone for refuge, together with his consort. // 203
To that God who conquered the gods together with Varuṇa and the guardians of wealth, / together with Brahmā, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, Viṣṇu, and Vāyu, / having Indra as chief, along with the sages possessing great weapons, / we have gone for refuge, together with his consort. // 204
Whatever impurity and evil was committed against you / out of ignorance, or out of attachment, fault, and delusion, / let Śarva, the soul of the universe, out of his noble nature / forgive all of that today for me together with my wife. // 205
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having praised the Lord of gods in this manner, his eyes turbid with tears, / stretching out his arms, he fell to the earth with his whole body. // 206
The mighty God himself, O fortunate one, then lifted up / that Dakṣa, who had surrendered with tear-clouded eyes, along with the Goddess. // 207
His tears fell upon the ground, turning into drops there.

Then the God spoke to that river of auspicious marks:
"Because you, O goddess, have issued from a drop of tear from Arjuna [Dakṣa], // 209
therefore you shall be famous by the auspicious name Arjunā.
O highly renowned one, you shall flow reaching festival after festival. // 210
And whoever bathes in you shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.

shall not obtain rebirth into human state nor a bad migration.

and feeds a brahmin after bathing in you, he too shall go

[Dakṣa] said: / "O ruler of the gods, let her become my daughter." // 228
Sanatkumāra said: / Saying "So be it," Umā gave that goddess as a daughter. / And saying "You are Death," he engaged her in dreadful work, // 229
the auspicious goddess, in taking away the breath of all living beings. / Appointed by Brahmā himself to perform that task, / with raised arms, along with the Lord of gods, always engaged by you and me. // 230
Whoever reads or listens to this matchless destruction of Dakṣa's sacrifice, / the establishment of Bhadreśvara, and the grace bestowed on Dakṣa, // 231
or recites it to twice-born [brahmins], / freed from all sins, is glorified in the heavenly world. // 232
To the one who cast down the eyes of Bhaga, the forest fire to Dakṣa's sacrifice, / the fire to Madana's city, whose body is radiant with the crescent moon, / the time of destruction for the sacrifice of the gods' priest, the guardian of the seven worlds— / to Śaṃkara I have gone for refuge for the sake of peace. // 233
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, the destruction of Dakṣa's sacrifice, in the Skandapurāṇa.

Grant our desired wishes, O Lord of the universe!"
Sanatkumāra said:
"Whoever praises [him] constantly with this, endowed with restraint,
endowed with all desires, shall attain the desired goal."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the God brought all those attendants back to their natural state,
and Nandin and the Goddess, and also himself.
And he said to the two of them: "I am pleased; let a desired boon be taken!"
The two gods said:
"If you are pleased, O Lord of gods, if a boon is to be granted to us two:
having attained another birth, may we two continually carry you, O Lord of gods!
And this secret place of ours, intensely sanctified by our austerity,
may it become holy by your grace, O Lord of gods!"
The God of gods said:
"This excellent place shall become my supreme secret.
Within merely the range of five arrow-shots, one who dies here shall indeed become a lord of the gaṇas.
Since I, Bhava, having stood in your midst, have been worshipped by you two,
therefore let this [place] become renowned by the name 'Madhyama'.
Attaining another birth, worshipped and immensely powerful,
becoming my mount, you two shall sustain the worlds."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having spoken thus to those two foremost gods,
the God went with the lords of the gaṇas to Mandara, which has golden caves.

7.4.m:
Then, when the God had departed together with his attendants, after a long time,
in this Manvantara, the auspicious Surabhī propitiated Rudra.
Gratified by her austerity of a thousand years, Bhava
gave darśana, O Vyāsa, and said: "I am a granter of boons."
She chose an incomparable son, the foremost of all living beings,
and other sons of great strength, worthy of sacrifice, foremost among the gods,
as well as other very beautiful daughters, sustainers of the world.
Then the God granted all and vanished from sight.
When that Mahādeva had departed, Surabhī gave birth to a son of blazing splendour,
the firstborn of all creatures, a bull;
and the sustainer of the world gave birth to the eleven Rudras, the auspicious younger brothers of the bull,
and to those seven daughters, the cows.
That bull, having met [them], always in the morning, having performed his daily rites,
having bowed to his father, his mother, and likewise to his grandfather,
the radiant one went to the forest frequented by the four world-elephants,
the abode of the hosts of Siddhas, where that divine dūrvā grass
arisen from ambrosia, tasting of nectar, springs up when cut or burnt.
Once, wandering in that forest, satisfied yet afflicted by thirst,
the king of bulls, the son of Surabhī, went to the ocean to drink.
Having plunged into the ocean, taking a great mouthful, he then, opening his huge mouth,
drank the sea water in its midst, with rage, together with the timiṅgilas,

7.4.m:
Then the lord ocean, being drunk down, was exceedingly distressed; / going to the submarine fire, he fled for refuge to the Saṃvarta fire. / And that fire of great might, exceedingly enraged, having granted him / safety, went up to the bull and, with joined palms, spoke thus:
Saṃvarta said: / 'This [ocean] is the refuge of all beings and the auspicious abode of the Daityas. / Powerful one, it does not befit you to deprive it of waters.'
The bull said: / 'Fire, it was not my intention to consume the ocean completely; / but since you are its protector, I shall certainly do so today!
Whatever pride and arrogance you have, whatever strength and whatever prowess, / show that to me, lord of oblations! I shall drink it before your very eyes.'
Sanatkumāra said: / Having spoken thus to the dweller of the submarine fire, the lord of bulls / impetuously set about drinking the ocean dry.

7.4.m:
Sanatkumāra said: / Having released the bull, fire went swiftly to his own abode. / The bull also went away, covered with distress and sorrow. / Disgraced, that radiant great bull, son of Surabhi, / his spirit crushed with grief, went along thinking thus: / 'I am weak, and fire is mighty, by whom I was humiliated in this way; / and though master of my life, he did not separate me from my breaths! / All my strength is in vain, and likewise my loud roar, / like that of an autumn cloud bereft of waters in the sky! / Today I shall cast off my life-breaths, restrained and resolved on a vow, / so that such a humiliation of my pride will never happen to me again. / For one who is subdued by an enemy, weak and wretched, / I consider death superior to life. What is the use of living?' / [Variant readings]
Sanatkumāra said: / As the bull was reflecting thus, he heard an auspicious voice from the sky: / 'Son of Surabhi, do not fear! Do what I tell you: /'

7.4.m:
'Take refuge in Rudra, the lord of all gods, stronger than all. / Seek refuge in that lord of gods; then you will conquer fire.'
'He is the creator of all beings, beginning with Brahmā, without a doubt; / he will dispel all this grief of yours, O bull!'
Sanatkumāra said: / Having heard this from the high-souled Sādhya, the bull of great splendor / went to the Himavant mountain and performed severe austerity.
After a thousand years of him who was devoted and whose desires were set thereon, / the lord, the master of all beings, accompanied by Ambā and his gaṇas, spoke:
The god of gods said: / 'Fortunate son of Surabhi, I am pleased with you, little son. / Ask for whatever desired boons, dear child; I shall grant them, even many.'

Sanatkumāra said:

wearing a crown and garlands, three-eyed, adorned with earrings and armlets, / broad-chested, armored, bow in hand, exceedingly powerful,

He said to that Rudra: "Go, bind the throbbing Saṃvartaka Fire / who dwells in the mouth of the Vaḍavā, and bring [him] here!"

7.4.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
Having bowed to the feet of Soma, the leader of the attendants / went swiftly to the ocean and saw the Fire.
Having fought a mighty, dreadful battle that made the hair stand on end, / he bound the Saṃvartaka Fire and brought him to the Lord's side.
Vyāsa said:
What was that battle like between the lord of the subjects and the Fire? / I wish to know this; tell [it], O best of speakers!
Sanatkumāra said:
Having gone there, that enraged leader of the attendants then spoke meaningful words / to the Saṃvartaka Fire, his eyes red with anger:
The leader of the attendants said:
"The master of the entire world, the god adorned with the crescent moon, / commands you, O Fire: propitiate this bull!
Say to the bull together with your friends, 'I bow [to you]'; / abide by his command and do whatever is to be done!"

Go, at my word tell the venerable three-eyed Lord: / If he tells me again, I shall then act accordingly."

7.4.m:
The lord of the attendants said:
"Foolish are they, alas, who, devoid of strength and knowledge, [think themselves] wise; / addressed in this way, they would go as you speak to me.
Single is the command of the strong; single, of the sovereign. / And he indeed is the best messenger who accomplishes his goal.
I, being powerful, have been dispatched here as a messenger / by that mighty creator of the worlds, the bearer of the Pināka, for the attainment of all purposes.
If you will not obey my word, then today I shall bind you / with great nooses as you throb, and lead you into the presence of the bearer of the moon!"

Sanatkumāra said:
Addressed thus, that fiery one, his eyes glowing like kindled fire, / rushed at the leader of the attendants, shouting: "Halt, halt!"
As he was rushing with speed, he who knew weapons, powerful, struck him with the weapon of Parjanya; / [yet] the swift one blazed forth.
As he approached nearby, blazing, overwhelmed with anger, / he struck him between the breasts with a mighty thunderbolt-weapon.

Struck then by that weapon, the lord of burning, swift though he was, was stunned; / agitated and smokeless, he stood still for a moment.
Then, overwhelmed with anger, the leader of the attendants bound the great Fire / with the noose of Rudra by both hands as he flared.
Seeing him bound by that excellent noose and fallen, / his sons and friends, hands bearing various weapons,
rushed at the leader of the attendants in anger by hundreds and thousands. / Having defeated them as well, the leader of the attendants swiftly brought that Fire
to Hara, like a consecrated sacrificial animal at a sacrifice. / Mahādeva, seeing that consumer of the ocean brought [before him],
spoke to the bull: "Speak, what should be done with him?" / Seeing him wretched and dejected in mind, the great bull,
bowing down his head to the feet, said this with joined palms: / "O venerable one, Lord of the Gods, Great Lord of all the worlds!

with his mouth split open to his ears, huge-bodied, exceedingly strong, / with arms like huge iron clubs, firm with a diamond-hard body, // 111
with huge fangs, a broad chest, holding a great sword and bow, / with eyes like glowing coals, three-eyed, radiant with armor, // 112
bearing exceedingly inexhaustible quivers, clad in an animal skin, / holding an arrow with one hand and a bow with the other; // 113
shining like the peak of Mount Meru with an upper garment resembling the sky, / variegated with planets and lunar mansions and illuminated by lightning and the sun. // 114
Addressing him distinctly as "Prabhākara," the Lord spoke / this to that Prabhākara in the presence of all the gods: // 115
"O Prabhākara, commanded by me, you mine of virtues for the gods, / endowed with supreme power, restrain the momentum of the bull! / And for your dwelling I give you the divine Indradvīpa. // 116
Jyotsnā shall be your wife, and likewise, free from old age and death, / you shall be my great leader of the gaṇas, as commanded by me." // 117
Sanatkumāra said: / Then all the deities, having bowed down to him together with Brahmā, / went to their own abodes; the God too, possessing the bull, shone forth. // 118
From the face upwards, the bull is Dharma; the hips are said to be the sacrifice; / the eyes are the moon and the sun, and Brahmā rests on the head. // 119
Varuṇa is on his tongue; Vāyu himself moves within. / Viṣṇu, Bhaga, Pūṣan, and Śakra dwell on his feet. // 120
The remaining sons of Diti reside on his shanks and thighs; / the Rudras reside on his ears, nose, neck, lips, and chin. // 121
His hooves are the weapons, and the discus and thunderbolt are on his horns; / Mitra himself is in his anus; the tail is gifts of all kinds. // 122
All the mountains are his bones; the auspicious Śrī was his dung; / and his urine, O Vyāsa, was heavenly, purifying nectar. // 123

7.4.m:
All the seers were his bodily hair, and the constellations in every direction; / his joints, O Vyāsa, were the auspiciously visible planets.
The sacrifices and Vedic rites, the mantras, hymns, and [their] fruits / became his flesh, and the rivers and oceans his blood.
The seven worlds were the mouth of that being of unequaled splendour; / the rays of light were his hands, and medicinal herbs indeed his marrow.
The sacrificial animals were born of mantras, [his] sinews the climbing plants, / creepers, trees, and shrubs, and likewise the other auspicious mountains.
The serpents were his blood-vessels, and the Vasus his accumulation of semen; / his stomach and intestines are remembered as the two divine Aśvins.
The clouds were his skin, and the garlands of lightning […]; / […] the yakṣas, gandharvas, and apsarases.
The veins, arteries, intoxication, and arrogance were born [from him]; / humans, the Mother Goddesses, and various kinds of spirits [too].

7.4.m:
This must never be given or recited to a deceitful person, / nor to an atheist, an evil-doer, or a sinner.
This should be given and recited to a son, a disciple, a righteous man, a great soul, / and to a pure person; this is an eternal secret.
May that Maheśa be always pleased with you, / who rides upon that [bull] who arose from the world and the Vedas, who accomplishes all aims, who is of great might, and who roars like rainclouds and the ocean.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, called ‘The Māhātmya of the Origin of the Bull’.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus, O Vyāsa, having given up the cloud, that lord, the ruler of gods, / came to have the bull as his mount, just as I have told you.

How did the blessed goddess, who was dark, attain fairness? / And what was the reason for it? Indeed, I wish to know this.
Sanatkumāra said:
Seated on the slope of Mount Mandara, Umā and the Destroyer of the Body of Kāma / sported then with the pramathas, who assumed various forms.
Then, as they played there, in the midst of conversation, / the blessed lady was called ‘Dark One’ by the god; at that the high-spirited goddess grew angry.
Embracing her who was angry, Mahādeva, of great splendour, / spoke at once, composed, consoling her with sweet words:

7.4.m:
Addressed thus, Girijā said: "When abundant austerity has been performed, / you alone, O Lord, are the giver of the boons desired by me."
Then, having made this petition to the one who sees the purpose of all actions, / and bowing to the feet of Śiva of boundless radiance,
the goddess arrived in a moment at Himavat, the best of mountains. / She saw it adorned with the hermitages of the foremost seers,
having reached Lake Mānasa and also that Lake Bindu, / the celestial white rock, and the source of the Gaṅgā.
Then, reaching Mahālaya and likewise the Devadāru forest,
and having arrived at other foremost forests after that, that virtuous woman, / going to the north of that mountain, exceedingly charming,
saw a single celestial peak secluded in solitude, / made of gold, heavenly, covered with all herbs,
with surfaces of beautiful sapphire, great sapphire, and blue lapis, / surrounded on all sides by wondrous trees of jewels.

Likewise, other trees [produced] many kinds of beds and ornaments; / and other trees produced bee-less honey equal to nectar.
Others produced various enjoyments and likewise ornaments; / some brought forth women, and others brought forth men.
All the ground on that celestial mountain was jewel-strewn; / a fragrant wind blew, neither excessively hot nor cold.
Even as the great goddess had not yet arrived at that mountain, / Rudra created it just then for the pleasure of the goddess.
And by his grace alone, that mountain was not accessible / to the hosts of all the gods, nor to any of the spirits anywhere.
Sanatkumāra said: / On that best of mountains, the goddess performed an austerity exceedingly difficult to perform, / wearing two charming garments made of bark as the means for Dharma.
At times she fed on fruit, at times she ate leaves; / at times she consumed water, at times she ate only wind.

From the ornaments she had earlier laid down on the lovely slab of rock / a river possessing holy waters was born. . .57. .

“This woman has been seen before by me beside Śarva, exceedingly beautiful. / From the kind of power her austerity shows, I deem she is no mortal woman. . .63. .
Or rather, she is always devoted to Maheśvara; / the daughter of the Himavat sports on Mount Mandara with the god. . .64. .
What need then does she have of austerity, whose husband is the holder of the Pināka? / This must be some other woman endowed with her form, committed to the vows of austerity. . .65. .
Endowed with great fiery splendor, this auspicious woman cannot be killed / by me today for food—she by whom I have been paralyzed and stopped. . .66. .
Therefore I will wait upon her until the passage of time. / Later, when this powerless woman has died of herself, / I, distressed by hunger, shall devour her at will, / as a sage [eats] a fruit in an hermitage.” / Having reflected thus, that tiger remained not far from the goddess, . .67–68. .

7.4.m: Rudra said: / "O highly fortunate Upamanyu, behold me, freed from feverish anxiety. / Decide in your mind and state a boon, so that I may grant it to you." / Sanatkumāra said: / Then, beholding the lord of gods and bowing with his head, / he, bowed low, spoke words, resolving in his mind: / "O Lord, if you are pleased, you who are ever worshipped by hosts of suras, / grant me what I say, O Īśāna; homage to you! / Without relying upon any worldly or divine substance, / may I eat milk-rice presented to me without begging." / The god of gods said: / "Here [in this world], nothing exists for anyone without relying [on something], O best of brahmins. / Having made even a blade of grass your support, speak therefore, O great sage." / Upamanyu said: / "I rely on nothing at all, O Lord, by your grace. / For that purpose was this undertaking; therefore grant what was requested!" / The god of gods said: "O sage, without relying on anything, there is no milk-rice for you." / Having said this to him, Mahādeva vanished right there.

Having vanished, the wielder of the Pināka bow, in order to test him, / assumed the form of Brahmā and then spoke to him again.
Brahmā said: / "O wise Upamanyu, your auspicious tapas has been well performed. / I am pleased with you; state a boon, and I shall bestow whatever you desire."
Upamanyu said: / "O Lord, ruler of all worlds, homage to you, creator of all, O master. / Well performed is my tapas, O god, since I behold you, guardian of the world. / I am a devotee of Maheśvara, dependent on his blessings, devoted to him. / From him I choose a boon, O god; not from you, without doubt."
Brahmā said: / "O brahmin, Rudra did not give you milk-rice, which is not difficult to obtain. / From where else, then, will he give you an excellent boon here? / The state of Prajāpati, or godhood, or immortality, / or the status of Indra, Soma, or Viṣṇu—I shall give to you!"

wearing a serpent as his sacred thread, clad in a tiger-skin garment, / with a black-antelope skin as an upper cloth, and holding a water pot; / carrying a staff, holding a trident, laughing loudly, surrounded by many gaṇa leaders, / he said: "Son! O son, I am pleased with your austerity!
Immortal, freed from old age, rid of all sorrow, / assuming any form at will, glorious—you shall become [all this] through my grace.
And take this island created by me, which moves at will, / surrounded on all sides by an ocean of milk-rice.
Endowed with the power of great yoga, all-knowing, pleasant to look upon, / always enjoy milk-rice together with your kinsmen, my child!

Salutations to the slayer of the enemies of the gods! Salutations indeed to the one of fierce impetuosity! / Salutations to the lord of the ancestors and gods! Salutations indeed to the destroyer of the sacrifice!

Sanatkumāra said:
Then that blessed God made Sukeśa, the leader of the gaṇas, / into a brahmin once again, O Vyāsa, dedicated to austerity and truth.
Vyāsa said:
How did he, previously a brahmin, attain leadership of the gaṇas? / Pleased with what austerity of his did the Lord bestow leadership of the gaṇas?
Sanatkumāra said:
There was a brahmin born of the lineage of Vasiṣṭha, truthful of speech, pure,
devoted to pilgrimages to sacred fords, and dedicated to fasting.
Once, when he was in a foreign land, he saw in a forest, standing on the path,
a tiger with its mouth wide open, terrible, bearing claws and fangs as weapons. // 3–4
Seeing it then, that brahmin quickly left the path
and entered a great, dreadful forest devoid of living beings. // 5
There he saw before him, clinging to a clump of vīraṇa grass,
men hanging downwards, weeping and utterly miserable. // 6
Seeing those twice-born hanging head-downwards then,
he asked, “Who are you?”, and they spoke this to him: // 7

7.4.m:
Men desire sons [thinking], “These [sons] will deliver us
from hell”; but you will cause us, who are miserable, to fall!
The brahmin said:
By the tapas that I have accumulated through visiting sacred fords,
and whatever good deed has been performed by me since birth,
by that, O grandfathers, deliver yourselves from this pit!
The ancestors said:
We cannot be delivered from this pit by tapas,
nor by sacrifices, nor otherwise; do that for us which we tell you! // 9–11 //
Produce offspring endowed with good qualities and possessed of tapas;
then we might be freed from this pit, if you consent. // 12
The brahmin said:
I have undertaken this vow, saying: “I am a celibate whose seed goes upward;
I shall not take wives, and yet I shall certainly deliver my ancestors.”
Then, abandoning them in that state, enveloped by great sorrow,
he went to Rudra for refuge; thereupon the ancestors vanished. // 13–14
When the ancestors had vanished in this way, the twice-born, subsisting on wind,
became like a piece of wood, a clod of earth, or a stone, and remained without breathing. // 15

7.4.m:
Fixing his mind upon Rudra, motionless, well concentrated,
whispering prayers to the Rudras with his heart, he stayed in the open air. // 16
[Variant readings]
Then, when a month was completed for him, there occurred a great storm of wind and rain
that agitated all creatures, unbearable, accompanied by a terrible roaring sound. // 17
By that great rainstorm, no suffering
nor any interruption happened to him then; he remained steadfastly composed. // 18

assuming the form of Viṣṇu, spoke to that best of the twice-born: // 19

“I am pleased with you; may it be well with you! By this tapas, O one of good vows,
choose a boon, O brahmin-seer, which is in your heart.” // 20
Then Sukeśa, seeing that Nārāyaṇa had arrived,
said: “I wish for a boon from Śaṃkara, indeed not from you.” // 21
Viṣṇu said:
Enough with this stubborn persistence directed towards Hara, O brahmin-seer!
He cannot be seen even by the gods, how much less by human beings? // 22
Sukeśa said:
Whether he can be seen or cannot be seen, what is the use of these deliberations of yours?
Whether I have a foolish obstinacy or a wise resolve, nevertheless my mind is set on the Lord. // 23
Only from Śaṃkara, O Lord of the discus, whether it brings good or ill,
do I desire a boon; not from you, nor from anyone else in any way. // 24
For since you all, firmly focused,
worship and praise that God, therefore he is called the highest. // 25

7.4.m:
And all these ancestors of yours, O sinless one, have been rescued from terrible hell by you, an excellent son, and have approached you, a leader of the Gaṇas. / They shall be your servants, eternally freed from suffering. These leaders of the Gaṇas shall indeed be subject to your command.
You shall be renowned by the name Sukeśa, / and endowed always with sovereignty of eightfold qualities, you shall roam.
Sanatkumāra said: / Then, seeing his ancestors together with their kinsmen rescued from hell, / and endowed once more with the venerable state of leaders of the Gaṇas,
with a delighted mind, having bowed his head with palms joined, he went to Maheśvara. / Then, his face joyful, skilled in speech, he spoke:
Sukeśa said: / O Lord, leadership of the Gaṇas and sovereignty indeed have been attained, / as well as imperishable immortality, and likewise the supreme freedom from old age. / And these ancestors have been rescued and made into leaders of the Gaṇas by me, / and this wish-going mountain has indeed been attained by me through your grace.

This I wish to hear from you, dear father, either in detail or in brief, in its true nature— / beneficial and conveying all happiness. / Sūta said: / Thus addressed, that lord, son of the creator of the gods, creator of aerial chariots, free of self-interest, / who increases the realm of the gods, spoke words concerning what was done in the past, destroying all evil deeds. / Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, named The Granting of Boons to Sukeśa, in the Skandapurāṇa. / Sanatkumāra said: / Seated upon the peak of Trikūṭa in that divine-built city, / in a celestial golden aerial chariot crowded with women,
having summoned all his ancestors and worshipped them according to the rules, / seeing them sitting comfortably, he spoke these words:

The ancestors said: / 'Do not speak an untruth thus, son, lest unrighteousness accrue to you here. / Your sovereignty is never from our grace, son. / We, however, being tormented in the terrible, very harsh hell, / have attained happiness hard to obtain through your austerity and prowess.
Just as we have been rescued from hell by you, an excellent son, / so we see no other [equal to you]; for fortunate are you, our son! / Today, for many thousands of years in the terrible hell, / we evil-doers would be cooking, were you not our kinsman.
Many living beings, son, are tormented there, bound fast, / in the exceedingly terrible [hell], very wicked people who possess no austerity.'

Because they perform that duty, and because they do not deviate from their own duty, / that properly observed righteousness generates auspicious offspring. // 13

You are the sustainer, you indeed are our relative, you are our progenitor, O wise one! / You alone are the father, and we are indeed your sons, there is no doubt. // 25
In this matter we shall relate to you an ancient event, O wise one, / sung in Śruti and Smṛti, which you ought to acknowledge on our behalf. // 26
The ancestors said:
Sons were indeed created by Brahmā, [saying], 'O gods, sacrifice unto me.' / They then sacrificed unto themselves; at them Brahmā was enraged. // 27
Enraged, he said to them: 'You shall lose your consciousness!' / Having been cursed by Brahmā, all those denizens of heaven gathered together, // 28
and, beset with sorrow and grief, miserable, they then praised him. / Perceiving that he was pleased, they, bowing with their heads, said: // 29
'We have lost our consciousness, O Lord; restore it to us again, O ruler! / And forgive that, O Lord of gods, which was done by us through ignorance.' // 30

That very awareness is no longer in us, O God, O Lord who creates all,
by which we might know those expiations, O protector of the world. (33)

and once more awareness, O knowers of duty; do not act otherwise. (34)

7.4.m:
The ancestors said:
Then those best among the gods questioned their own sons at that time
about the expiations, the duties, and the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences in detail. (35)
And then those sons, pure and auspicious, declared all that to them
faithfully and in true order, through supreme concentration. (36)
Then, having regained awareness and likewise having attained their desires,
they addressed their own sons, rejoicing and filled with delight. (37)
The gods said:
You are not our sons; we indeed are your sons, your offspring,
by whom imperishable knowledge was granted unto us whose awareness was lost. (38)
When they had spoken thus, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, arrived there,
and that one of great renown said this to all those gods: (39)
Brahmā said:
The gods do not speak untruth; truth abides among the gods.
All of them have indeed been called your sons and ancestors; that is not untruth. (40)

7.4.m:
Therefore, fatherhood over you for your sons shall be eternal and imperishable,
there is no doubt, and you are their sons in every respect. (41)
For secret doctrines are never taught to a non-pupil;
and 'son' and 'pupil' have the same meaning; therefore you are sons in every respect. (42)
Fathers cross over by means of sons, and they cause those sons to cross over as well;
having brought about crossing-over, they attain the status of fathers by virtue of that deed. (43)
And you have been made to cross over from ignorance and also from hell by your sons;
therefore, these are the fathers, and you are sons in every respect. (44)
Because he protects, he is a father; or because he begets, he is a father;
and both of these apply to the sons; on that account they are considered your fathers. (45)
Then they, Brahmā […]
[…] (46)
[…] of might.
The fathers gratified them with chosen boons, undisturbed. (47)
And then the fathers chose for themselves worship prior [to the gods]:
'Whoever sacrifices to the gods without having sacrificed to us shall not obtain that fruit, (48)
and joined with guilt, a great […]
[…] (49)
[…]
Then they went back as they had come along with Brahmā in every direction. (50)
The fathers said:
Just as we, having lost our senses, were made to cross over
from hell by you, O son, endowed with consciousness, and made foremost once again, (51)
therefore you, as a father, are worthy of worship, who follow [the law], O great […]
[…] (52)
[…], best of virtuous beings,
bowing down with joined palms, spoke these words to the fathers: (53)
'It is so, exactly as you have said; your auspicious word is no falsehood.
For mutual fatherhood has indeed been declared for all. (54)
Grant me further this boon, O lords of the hosts:
[…]
By this the desired question has indeed been spoken, O best of brahmins(?).' (55)

7.4.m:
The fathers said:
Nothing is unknown to you, O lord of the foremost.
You desire to explain the truth here for the sake of our authority. (56)
Speak what is known to us; we shall indeed tell it to you,
either heard or experienced, according to our ability, accurately. (57)
Sukeśa said:
You were tormented in the dreadful, extremely severe hell;
hence you know from tradition all the hells, without a doubt. (58)
Their true nature, conjunction, division of time, and succession—
all that I wish to hear, for my curiosity is very great. (59)
How many are those hells, of what size are they, what do they rest upon,
of what form are they, and who are punished [there], and how, deeply afflicted? (60)

7.4.m:
Soma, Agni, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Sūrya— / the witnesses of living beings there declare what was done and left undone by that man.
Addressed, convicted, and reproached by Citragupta, / the tormented man is cast into hell with feet above and head below.
With javelins having exceedingly sharp points, with arrows, with battle-axes, / with slings, with mallets, with spears inflicting deep wounds,
with iron clubs, with saws, with thunderbolts, with chisels, with stone hammers, / with spikes, with pestles, and indeed with caustic powder;
and with blazing, terrible weapons, and even with a rain of fire, / being beaten day and night, crying out piteously in manifold ways,
after a thousand years he reaches a ‘propitious’ hell. / Having fallen there, being tormented again, intensely miserable,
without rest for a crore of years, he reaches the end of hell. / Freed from the great hell, he takes resort to another elevation.

that creature is reborn in worldly existence as a worm, an insect, and the like. / But those vilest of men who go to those terrible hells,

Men bound for the great hell are tormented there: / two mountains crowded with great beasts, lions, and tigers,
thronged with śarabhas and elephants, crowded with numerous serpents, / with birds of diverse forms, and with men holding uplifted weapons,
provided with leafless trees bearing needles of adamantine thorns; / between the two is a level ground covered with needles,
pointing upwards, with adamantine tips, and truly impenetrable; / surrounded on the other side by terrifying men with weapons in hand,
and completely enclosed all around by an iron rampart; / and in the sky, those two are covered by an iron net.

7.4.m:
Men are tortured there who indeed assault
an unwilling woman belonging to another, and also the defiler of a maiden,
the stealer of deposits, and likewise the stealer of meat,
the stealer of sap, and also whoever reviles others,
the slayer of the host of sense organs, and likewise the wearer of false marks,
the hunter of wild animals and beasts, and those who eat flesh from behind [the back of others],
those who eat meat in vain, and those who commit violence:
these vilest of men, my son, go to Yamalācala.
And when twin [children] are born, whichever vilest of men does not perform
expiation, being impure of mind, he too reaches it.
Harried by those men as described,
and cut down by weapons, he reaches that mountain.
There he is devoured by enraged tigers, śarabhas, and hyenas,
by serpents, wild cats, and birds with iron beaks.
And if, being devoured by them, he climbs a tree,
there he is pierced by sharp thorns and by birds.
Then, if he desires to go into a crevice or a cave of it,
even there, burned by fire, afflicted with pain, he turns back.
Then, if he enters into the terrible interval between the two,
there the man is pierced in both feet by fierce needles.

Being thus tortured indeed for many years, in great misery,
finding an exit and escaping, he is thrown down upon high peaks.
Whoever regularly listens to this Yamalācala of terrible impetus,
which brings manifold sinful retribution, he never goes to that terrible sinful state.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, called the Description of Yamalācala in the account of the hells, in the Skandapurāṇa.

Suśarman said:
Next I shall describe the Śālmalī hell again,
where men who are evil-doers are excessively tortured.
There are many thousands of silk-cotton trees, O best of lords,
all of them tall, dreadful, and extending over many yojanas.
Endowed with great branches, large leaves, and huge thorns,
they are enclosed on all sides by a vast wall of iron.
All of them are covered above with a vast net.
Many men with angry faces stand there,
holding thunderbolt-bludgeons and stones, carrying swords and clubs,
with hands armed with various other kinds of weapons.
Those cruel ones excessively torture the helpless creatures.
Being slashed even there by rākṣasas of cruel deeds,
he flees in all directions, stricken with pain, exceedingly miserable.
Wherever he goes, there he is struck down.
Approaching him fallen into pits, the exceedingly dreadful
rākṣasas cut him to pieces from all sides with weapons of various shapes,

7.4.m:
Measuring repeatedly with the great Kālasūtra ('thread of time/death'), / they severely hack off the limbs of creatures of evil deeds with blunt-edged weapons.
By those attendants, without rest, unwearied day and night, / when the time is complete, the creature reaches the heights. / Having rested then, that creature is cast down into hell again / until every bit of the sin committed by him is completely exhausted.
Whoever listens to this thread describing many sin-doers and the deeds of the world that are hard to bear, / does not go to that hell of fierce suffering, that Kālasūtra of the realm of Yama.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, in the description of the hells, named 'Kālasūtra'.

One who bakes bricks, and likewise one who bakes clay pots, / and one who destroys them; one who sets fire to houses, . . 5 . . / or in a forest, on a threshing floor, or in a cow-pen; one who destroys food and drink; / one who causes obstacles at meals; one who spoils sacrifices, one who burns sacrifices; . . 6 . . / and one who performs deceitful deeds, and likewise a false witness; / one who builds a sacrificial altar falsely, and likewise one who brings fire falsely; . . 7 . . / one who offers improperly cooked food; and one who disparages the Vedas; / and that vilest of men who steals the tools of artisans— . . 8 . . / thus tortured there, having again obtained a rest on the heights, / they fall down once more into hell, until the end of their destruction. . . 9 . . / That human being who hears this ripening of many sins, this ripening of karma, / does not go to that hell of the wicked's ripening, the Kumbhīpāka filled with torturing misery. . . 8.40.10 . .
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, named Kumbhīpāka, in the description of hells in the Skandapurāṇa.

They are superior in sharpness and in cutting, O highly intelligent one. / Those [trees] are covered with such leaves and are thorny. (4) / Creatures bound there by sinful deeds by rākṣasas, / being beaten with sword-blades, clubs, and other great weapons, (5)
and scorched by fire, flee to those trees. / Seeing them arrived, the leaves fall down upon them; (6)
very heavy and sharp, they cut them to pieces. / With their heads and necks severed, they flee from that place. (7)
Having gone, they are tormented again and again by rākṣasas and unreachable trees / for fifty million years, intensely sorrowful. (8) / Then, released from them, they indeed enter the heights. / Having rested there, all of them [fall] from the heights into hell again. (9)
Helpless and bewildered, they are cast down until their sin is exhausted. / But as for those sinful men who go to that terrible hell, (10)

7.4.m:
I shall declare them to you; listen attentively, O twice-born: / the evil-minded one who destroys a tree that was raised like a son, (11)
or the evil-minded one who sells a tree grown / in an orchard or a village, in a hermitage, or on a path, (12) / or at a reservoir, in a garden, or in temples, / in a house, at a water-kiosk, on a riverbank, or at a crossroads, (13)
the evil-minded one who destroys trees grown anywhere whatsoever, / or bushes, creepers, shrubs, and even grasses, (14) / the fool who destroys them for the sake of shade, flowers, or fruit, / or to accomplish his own work, he falls into that [hell]. (15)

7.4.m:
And he who takes roots, flowers, and fruits / for himself to fulfill desire, and not for the sake of gods or ancestors, (16)
and the lowest of men who dams a river, fills up wells, / or cuts down a tree for its leaves or bark, / or destroys that tree—he falls into that [hell]. (17) / And he who severely harasses creatures that have settled in the shade, (18a-b)
or frightens and drives away those that have reached his own abode, (18c-d) / all of them go to that great hell of heights. / And having emerged from there, those unwholesome ones enter saṃsāra again. (19) / Whoever, with vigilant mind, listens to this hell that is the source of suffering for evildoers, (20a-b)
he of meritorious deeds, knowing the self, does not go to that hell named Asipatra. (20c-d) / Thus ends the forty-first chapter, named Asipatravana, in the description of hells in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.4.m:
Hereafter, listen attentively, O son, to the river Vaitaraṇī, / which destroys sins and brings terror to those of sinful deeds. (1) / The river Vaitaraṇī, O son, whose banks are cut as if by chisels, [though called] auspicious, / is filled with hair, bones, and blood, and is full of burning alkali. (2)
It is crowded with ullumpakas, gardabhakas, sea-monsters, tortoises, / porpoises, crocodiles, water-spiders, and rākṣasas, (3) / large-fanged, large-bodied, flesh-eating; / and it is surrounded by those Asipatra trees growing on its banks. (4)
